headline: With every lane on its own best practice the field converges near 1.6M renders/s, and next-yak's automatic CSS-variable path costs about 2× against the inline style the other lanes write by hand.

microbench.why: Lanes without native dynamic-value support split the static class from the moving value by hand, and it works: `cnfast` reaches 1.64M renders/s from 566,000 on the naive pattern, `panda` 1.00M from 218,000, `goober` 846,000 from 160,000. `next-yak-css` leads at 1.64M without anyone writing that split, because the compiler performs it. The styled lane takes a different route and pays for it: `next-yak` at 804,000 passes the value through a CSS custom property on a wrapper, 2.006 ms of SSR CPU against 0.730 ms for the css prop. The convergence is real, and so is what reaching it costs — a manual optimization repeated for every dynamic value in the codebase.

autocannon.why: `next-yak-css` at 1,301 req/s leads. The hand-written split rescues the runtime lanes under load as well: `styled-components` reaches 640 req/s against 218 on the naive pattern, and `goober` 764 against 158.

attribution.why: `next-yak-css` at 0.730 ms and `vanilla` at 0.732 ms hold the floor. `next-yak` at 2.006 ms is the slowest compile-time lane in the case, and what it pays for is the custom-property wrapper rather than any per-instance serialization. `emotion` at 2.50 ms stays the ceiling even with the hand-written split applied.

hydrate.why: The naive pattern's hydration cliff disappears: `goober` needs 80.2 ms here against 1,246 ms on `dyn-translate`. Six lanes finish between 44.5 ms and 48.3 ms.

inp.why: Fourteen lanes answer between 7.0 ms and 8.1 ms, flat at this spread. Changing a value on one element is cheap however the value is authored.

mount.why: `next-yak-css` at 59.3 ms leads a band running to 75.2 ms for twelve lanes. `goober` mounts in 78.7 ms against 1,223 ms on the naive pattern, the same rescue hydration shows.

renderTiming.why: One style recalculation per lane, 0.101 ms to 0.188 ms. Moving the value out of the selector holds the engine's matching work constant.

payload.why: `vanilla` at 5,502 gz B is the floor and the compile-time lanes sit just above it. The hand-written split fixes the wire too: `emotion` ships 18.4 kB here against 39.4 kB on the naive pattern and `styled-components` 18.9 kB against 35.5 kB, because one static rule replaces a thousand unique ones.

nsweep.why: `next-yak-css` at 2.47 ms and `vanilla` at 2.47 ms hold a flat line to the largest size, with the utility lanes joining at 2.56 ms and 2.64 ms. `next-yak` at 5.06 ms carries its custom-property cost as a slope, and `emotion` at 10.1 ms stays the steepest.

crossCase: The trio reads as one argument. The Example `dyn-translate` shown above is the naive pattern, what a codebase produces when nobody optimizes: `goober` at 160,000 renders/s and a 1.25 s hydration. This case is every lane at its best, and for a library without native dynamic-value support that best is hand-written, the developer splitting static class from inline style per component, for every dynamic value, indefinitely. next-yak ships that separation as a compiler feature instead. The Example `dyn-inline` shown below removes the last variable by putting every lane, next-yak included, on a plain inline style, and `next-yak` renders 1.65M there against 804,000 here, which prices its CSS-variable path at 2.05×.
